1	// Package review — see env.go for package-level rationale.
2	//
3	// tui_model.go provides reviewTUIModel, the Bubble Tea Model for the
4	// review dashboard. The model renders a per-agent status table
5	// during the run and supports Ctrl+O drill-in mode for inspecting one agent's
6	// live event buffer on the alt screen.
7	package review
8	
9	import (
10		"context"
11		"errors"
12		"fmt"
13		"strconv"
14		"strings"
15		"sync"
16		"time"
17	
18		"charm.land/bubbles/v2/spinner"
19		"charm.land/bubbles/v2/viewport"
20		tea "charm.land/bubbletea/v2"
21		"charm.land/lipgloss/v2"
22	
23		reviewtypes "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/review/types"
24		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/stringutil"
25	)
26	
27	// Default terminal dimensions used before the first tea.WindowSizeMsg
28	// arrives. Shared by the constructor and the dashboardWidth /
29	// detailViewportWidth fallbacks so both views render at the same width when
30	// termWidth is uninitialized — a 1-cell viewport falls back here would
31	// collapse to a single column, which is not what we want.
32	const (
33		defaultTermWidth  = 80
34		defaultTermHeight = 24
35	)
36	
37	// agentRow holds per-agent live state during the TUI run.
38	type agentRow struct {
39		name     string
40		status   reviewtypes.AgentStatus
41		runStart time.Time          // stamped on first event from this agent
42		runEnd   time.Time          // stamped on Finished/RunError event
43		tokens   reviewtypes.Tokens // cumulative
44		preview  string             // latest AssistantText preview, capped by display width
45		buffer   []reviewtypes.Event
46		err      error
47	}
48	
49	// agentEventMsg is sent to the Bubble Tea program when an agent emits an event.
50	type agentEventMsg struct {
51		agent string
52		ev    reviewtypes.Event
53	}
54	
55	// runFinishedMsg is sent when the orchestrator calls RunFinished.
56	type runFinishedMsg struct {
57		summary reviewtypes.RunSummary
58	}
59	
60	// tickMsg triggers spinner and duration column updates.
61	type tickMsg time.Time
62	
63	// reviewTUIModel is the Bubble Tea model for the review dashboard.
64	type reviewTUIModel struct {
65		rows       []agentRow
66		rowIdx     map[string]int // agent name → row index (O(1) lookup)
67		detailMode bool
68		detailIdx  int // which agent is shown in drill-in
69		// detail is the pager backing the drill-in body. Width/Height are kept
70		// in sync with termWidth/termHeight (minus header+footer). Scroll
71		// position is internal state; AtBottom drives auto-tail.
72		detail viewport.Model
73	
74		cancel     context.CancelFunc
75		cancelOnce *sync.Once
76	
77		spinner    spinner.Model
78		termWidth  int
79		termHeight int
80	
81		finished bool
82		summary  reviewtypes.RunSummary
83	
84		// cancelling tracks whether a Ctrl+C-initiated cancellation is in flight.
85		// Set true on the first Ctrl+C (in tandem with cancelOnce firing the shared
86		// CancelFunc); the dashboard switches to a "cancelling" indicator and the
87		// footer offers a force-quit hint. A second Ctrl+C while cancelling=true
88		// force-quits without waiting for agents to drain.
89		cancelling bool
90	}
91	
92	// newReviewTUIModel builds an initial model pre-populated with one row per
93	// agent. cancel is the shared CancelFunc; it must be the same one passed to
94	// NewTUISink.
95	func newReviewTUIModel(agents []string, cancel context.CancelFunc) reviewTUIModel {
96		sp := spinner.New()
97		sp.Spinner = spinner.Dot
98		sp.Style = lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(lipgloss.Color("8"))
99	
100		rows := make([]agentRow, len(agents))
101		rowIdx := make(map[string]int, len(agents))
102		for i, name := range agents {
103			rows[i] = agentRow{
104				name:   name,
105				status: reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown,
106			}
107			rowIdx[name] = i
108		}
109		// Seed viewport with defaults that match termWidth/termHeight so an
110		// immediate Ctrl+O before any WindowSizeMsg still renders.
111		vp := viewport.New(
112			viewport.WithWidth(defaultTermWidth),
113			viewport.WithHeight(defaultTermHeight-2),
114		)
115		return reviewTUIModel{
116			rows:       rows,
117			rowIdx:     rowIdx,
118			detail:     vp,
119			cancel:     cancel,
120			cancelOnce: &sync.Once{},
121			spinner:    sp,
122			termWidth:  defaultTermWidth,
123			termHeight: defaultTermHeight,
124		}
125	}
126	
127	// tickCmd schedules the next tick for duration/spinner refresh.
128	func tickCmd() tea.Cmd {
129		return tea.Tick(100*time.Millisecond, func(t time.Time) tea.Msg {
130			return tickMsg(t)
131		})
132	}
133	
134	// Init returns the initial spinner tick command.
135	func (m reviewTUIModel) Init() tea.Cmd {
136		return tea.Batch(m.spinner.Tick, tickCmd())
137	}
138	
139	// Update handles all incoming messages.
140	func (m reviewTUIModel) Update(msg tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
141		switch msg := msg.(type) {
142		case agentEventMsg:
143			return m.handleAgentEvent(msg)
144	
145		case runFinishedMsg:
146			m.finished = true
147			m.summary = msg.summary
148			// Sync each row's status from the orchestrator's summary. The
149			// in-stream events (Finished / RunError) update status as they
150			// arrive, but the orchestrator's classifyStatus has access to
151			// process-level signals (Wait error, ctx cancellation) that the
152			// event stream never surfaces. Without this sync, an agent that
153			// the orchestrator classified Cancelled (Ctrl+C path, no Finished
154			// emitted) or Failed (process exit non-zero, no Finished emitted)
155			// would still render as "running" in the final frame.
156			//
157			// Preserve any already-set status from the event stream — if the
158			// stream said Failed (RunError), the summary may say Succeeded
159			// (process exit 0); RunError stickiness wins. Only overwrite when
160			// the row is still in AgentStatusUnknown.
161			now := time.Now()
162			for i, run := range msg.summary.AgentRuns {
163				if i >= len(m.rows) {
164					break
165				}
166				if m.rows[i].status == reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown {
167					m.rows[i].status = run.Status
168				}
169				if run.Tokens.In > 0 || run.Tokens.Out > 0 {
170					m.rows[i].tokens = run.Tokens
171				}
172				if m.rows[i].err == nil && run.Err != nil {
173					m.rows[i].err = run.Err
174				}
175				if m.rows[i].runEnd.IsZero() && !m.rows[i].runStart.IsZero() {
176					m.rows[i].runEnd = now
177				}
178			}
179			return m, nil
180	
181		case tickMsg:
182			if m.finished {
183				return m, nil
184			}
185			var spinCmd tea.Cmd
186			m.spinner, spinCmd = m.spinner.Update(msg)
187			return m, tea.Batch(spinCmd, tickCmd())
188	
189		case spinner.TickMsg:
190			if m.finished {
191				return m, nil
192			}
193			var spinCmd tea.Cmd
194			m.spinner, spinCmd = m.spinner.Update(msg)
195			return m, spinCmd
196	
197		case tea.WindowSizeMsg:
198			wasAtBottom := m.detail.AtBottom()
199			m.termWidth = msg.Width
200			m.termHeight = msg.Height
201			m.detail.SetWidth(m.detailViewportWidth())
202			m.detail.SetHeight(m.detailViewportHeight())
203			m = m.refreshDetailContentWithAutoTail(wasAtBottom)
204			return m, nil
205	
206		case tea.KeyPressMsg:
207			return m.handleKey(msg)
208	
209		case tea.MouseWheelMsg, tea.MouseClickMsg, tea.MouseReleaseMsg, tea.MouseMotionMsg:
210			// Mouse events: only meaningful inside the drill-in viewport, which
211			// handles tea.MouseWheelMsg natively.
212			// Without this delegation the events arrive at the Program (because
213			// View.MouseMode = MouseModeCellMotion is set during detail mode)
214			// but fall through Update unhandled — the user sees no scroll
215			// response to the wheel.
216			if m.detailMode {
217				var cmd tea.Cmd
218				m.detail, cmd = m.detail.Update(msg)
219				return m, cmd
220			}
221			return m, nil
222		}
223		return m, nil
224	}
225	
226	// detailViewportWidth returns the viewport's width, mirroring termWidth.
227	func (m reviewTUIModel) detailViewportWidth() int {
228		width, _ := m.currentTerminalSize()
229		return width
230	}
231	
232	// detailViewportHeight returns the viewport's body height, reserving one line
233	// for the header and one for the footer.
234	func (m reviewTUIModel) detailViewportHeight() int {
235		_, termHeight := m.currentTerminalSize()
236		h := termHeight - 2
237		if h < 1 {
238			return 1
239		}
240		return h
241	}
242	
243	// refreshDetailContent re-renders the focused agent's events into the
244	// viewport. It preserves auto-tail: if the viewport was sitting at the bottom
245	// (or has no scrollable content), it jumps to the new bottom after the content
246	// is replaced; otherwise the user's scroll position is left untouched.
247	//
248	// reviewTUIModel uses value receivers throughout (matching the Bubble Tea
249	// idiom of returning an updated tea.Model from Update); the viewport is
250	// mutated in place on the returned copy and the caller assigns the result
251	// back.
252	func (m reviewTUIModel) refreshDetailContent() reviewTUIModel {
253		return m.refreshDetailContentWithAutoTail(m.detail.AtBottom())
254	}
255	
256	func (m reviewTUIModel) refreshDetailContentWithAutoTail(wasAtBottom bool) reviewTUIModel {
257		if len(m.rows) == 0 || m.detailIdx < 0 || m.detailIdx >= len(m.rows) {
258			m.detail.SetContentLines(nil)
259			return m
260		}
261		lines := buildEventLines(m.rows[m.detailIdx].buffer, m.detailViewportWidth())
262		m.detail.SetContentLines(lines)
263		if wasAtBottom {
264			m.detail.GotoBottom()
265		}
266		return m
267	}
268	
269	// handleAgentEvent processes an agentEventMsg, updating the relevant row.
270	func (m reviewTUIModel) handleAgentEvent(msg agentEventMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
271		idx, ok := m.rowIdx[msg.agent]
272		if !ok {
273			return m, nil
274		}
275		row := &m.rows[idx]
276	
277		// Stamp run-start on the first event from this agent (per-row, not
278		// TUI-start; prevents inflated durations for late-starting agents).
279		if row.runStart.IsZero() {
280			row.runStart = time.Now()
281		}
282	
283		row.buffer = append(row.buffer, msg.ev)
284	
285		switch e := msg.ev.(type) {
286		case reviewtypes.Started:
287			// runStart already set; no other state update needed.
288		case reviewtypes.AssistantText:
289			collapsed := stringutil.CollapseWhitespace(sanitizeDisplayText(e.Text))
290			row.preview = truncateDisplayWidth(collapsed, 80)
291		case reviewtypes.Tokens:
292			row.tokens = e // cumulative: overwrite, not sum
293		case reviewtypes.Finished:
294			// RunError is sticky: if a prior RunError event already classified
295			// this row as Failed, a subsequent Finished{Success: true} must NOT
296			// flip it back to Succeeded. CU3's parser-fix-loop guarantees that
297			// RunError + Finished{Success:false} both accompany torn streams;
298			// matching that contract here keeps the TUI consistent with
299			// classifyStatus from CU4 (which honors sawRunError).
300			if row.status != reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed {
301				if e.Success {
302					row.status = reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded
303				} else {
304					row.status = reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed
305				}
306			}
307			row.runEnd = time.Now()
308		case reviewtypes.RunError:
309			row.status = reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed
310			row.err = e.Err
311			if row.runEnd.IsZero() {
312				row.runEnd = time.Now()
313			}
314		case reviewtypes.ToolCall:
315			// No visible state update for tool calls in the dashboard.
316		}
317	
318		// Re-render the focused agent's viewport content when a new event lands
319		// for it. refreshDetailContent's AtBottom check preserves user scroll if
320		// they've scrolled up; auto-tails otherwise.
321		if m.detailMode && m.detailIdx == idx {
322			m = m.refreshDetailContent()
323		}
324	
325		return m, nil
326	}
327	
328	// handleKey processes keyboard input.
329	func (m reviewTUIModel) handleKey(msg tea.KeyPressMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
330		// Post-finish: explicit exit keys dismiss the TUI from either the
331		// dashboard or detail mode. Esc retains its "back to dashboard" meaning
332		// while drilled in so the user can return to the finished dashboard
333		// before quitting. Other keys (including Ctrl+O and scroll keys) fall
334		// through to normal handling so post-mortem inspection still works.
335		if m.finished {
336			switch {
337			case msg.Mod == 0 && msg.Code == 'q':
338				return m, tea.Quit
339			case msg.Mod == 0 && msg.Code == tea.KeyEnter:
340				return m, tea.Quit
341			case msg.Mod == tea.ModCtrl && msg.Code == 'c':
342				return m, tea.Quit
343			case msg.Mod == 0 && (msg.Code == tea.KeyEscape):
344				if !m.detailMode {
345					return m, tea.Quit
346				}
347				// Detail mode: fall through to main switch where Esc returns to dashboard.
348			}
349		}
350	
351		switch {
352		case msg.Code == 'c' && msg.Mod == tea.ModCtrl:
353			if m.cancelling {
354				// Second Ctrl+C while a cancellation is already in flight
355				// force-quits without waiting for agents to drain. Checked
356				// before m.detailMode so the force-quit escape hatch works
357				// from drill-in too — the dashboard footer hint promises this
358				// path and a user drilled into a hanging agent's buffer is
359				// exactly when they need force-quit most. cancelOnce guards
360				// CancelFunc against the duplicate-firing case.
361				return m, tea.Quit
362			}
363			if m.allAgentsTerminal() {
364				// Race window: every agent emitted a terminal event but
365				// runFinishedMsg hasn't arrived yet. There's nothing left to
366				// cancel — quit immediately instead of flashing the
367				// "Cancelling agents..." footer until the runFinishedMsg lands.
368				// Checked before m.detailMode so the user reading a finished
369				// agent's buffer doesn't have to press Esc first to dismiss.
370				return m, tea.Quit
371			}
372			if m.detailMode {
373				// Idle drill-in with at least one agent still running: Ctrl+C
374				// is intentionally ignored so the user reading content can't
375				// accidentally fire a cancel. Esc first to return to the
376				// dashboard.
377				return m, nil
378			}
379			m.cancelling = true
380			m.cancelOnce.Do(m.cancel)
381			// Do NOT quit on the first Ctrl+C: leave the TUI up so the user sees
382			// the cancelling indicator while agents drain. Natural finish
383			// (runFinishedMsg) or a second Ctrl+C dismisses the TUI.
384			return m, nil
385	
386		case msg.Code == 'o' && msg.Mod == tea.ModCtrl:
387			if m.detailMode {
388				m.detailMode = false
389				return m, nil
390			}
391			m.detailMode = true
392			if len(m.rows) > 0 && (m.detailIdx < 0 || m.detailIdx >= len(m.rows)) {
393				m.detailIdx = 0
394			}
395			// Resize viewport in case termWidth/termHeight have changed since
396			// last detail-mode entry, then load the focused agent's events and
397			// tail to the bottom.
398			m.detail.SetWidth(m.detailViewportWidth())
399			m.detail.SetHeight(m.detailViewportHeight())
400			m = m.refreshDetailContent()
401			m.detail.GotoBottom()
402			return m, nil
403	
404		case msg.Code == tea.KeyEscape:
405			if m.detailMode {
406				m.detailMode = false
407				return m, nil
408			}
409			return m, nil
410	
411		case msg.Code == tea.KeyLeft:
412			if m.detailMode && len(m.rows) > 0 {
413				m.detailIdx = (m.detailIdx - 1 + len(m.rows)) % len(m.rows)
414				m = m.refreshDetailContent()
415				m.detail.GotoBottom()
416			}
417			return m, nil
418	
419		case msg.Code == tea.KeyRight:
420			if m.detailMode && len(m.rows) > 0 {
421				m.detailIdx = (m.detailIdx + 1) % len(m.rows)
422				m = m.refreshDetailContent()
423				m.detail.GotoBottom()
424			}
425			return m, nil
426		}
427	
428		// Delegate any unhandled key to the viewport so PgUp/PgDn/Home/End/↑/↓
429		// reach its internal keymap. Only meaningful in detail mode — on the
430		// dashboard the viewport is inert.
431		if m.detailMode {
432			var cmd tea.Cmd
433			m.detail, cmd = m.detail.Update(msg)
434			return m, cmd
435		}
436		return m, nil
437	}
438	
439	// allAgentsTerminal reports whether every agent row has reached a terminal
440	// status. Used to short-circuit Ctrl+C cancellation in the race window between
441	// the last agent emitting Finished/RunError and runFinishedMsg arriving — at
442	// that point CancelFunc has nothing to do and the "Cancelling agents..."
443	// footer would only flash briefly before runFinishedMsg dismisses it anyway.
444	func (m reviewTUIModel) allAgentsTerminal() bool {
445		if len(m.rows) == 0 {
446			return false
447		}
448		for _, r := range m.rows {
449			if r.status == reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown {
450				return false
451			}
452		}
453		return true
454	}
455	
456	// View renders the current state.
457	//
458	// In detail mode we enable [tea.MouseModeCellMotion] so the embedded
459	// [viewport.Model] receives mouse-wheel events natively — the viewport handles
460	// them as scroll, but only if the Bubble Tea program is configured to deliver
461	// mouse messages. Bubble Tea v2 expresses that config as a per-view field
462	// rather than a Program option, so it lives here next to AltScreen.
463	// Dashboard mode leaves the default [tea.MouseModeNone] in place so normal
464	// terminal mouse selection still works on the summary table.
465	func (m reviewTUIModel) View() tea.View {
466		var content string
467		termWidth, termHeight := m.currentTerminalSize()
468		if m.detailMode && len(m.rows) > 0 {
469			content = detailFrame(m.rows[m.detailIdx], m.detail.View(), termWidth, termHeight)
470		} else {

532	func (m reviewTUIModel) renderRow(row agentRow) string {
533		name := row.name
534	
535		var statusStr string
536		switch row.status {
537		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded:
538			statusStr = "✓ done"
539		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed:
540			statusStr = "✗ failed"
541		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled:
542			statusStr = "— cancel"
543		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown:
544			switch {
545			case m.cancelling:
546				// In-flight cancellation: distinct from the terminal Cancelled
547				// state ("— cancel") so the user can see that the cancel signal

549				statusStr = "cancelling"
550			case row.runStart.IsZero():

552			default:
553				statusStr = m.spinner.View() + " running"
554			}
555		}
556	
557		durStr := ""
558		if !row.runStart.IsZero() {
559			if !row.runEnd.IsZero() {
560				durStr = formatDuration(row.runEnd.Sub(row.runStart))
561			} else {
562				durStr = formatDuration(time.Since(row.runStart))
563			}
564		}
565	
566		tokStr := ""
567		if row.tokens.In > 0 || row.tokens.Out > 0 {
568			tokStr = fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", formatCompact(row.tokens.In), formatCompact(row.tokens.Out))
569		}
570	
571		preview := row.preview

573			preview = stringutil.CollapseWhitespace(sanitizeDisplayText(formatErrorPreview(row.err)))
574		}

576		return m.renderTableLine(name, statusStr, durStr, tokStr, preview)

579	func formatErrorPreview(err error) string {
580		if err == nil {
581			return ""
582		}
583		var pe *reviewtypes.ProcessError
584		if errors.As(err, &pe) {
585			// Strip ANSI before the empty check — agents like codex/claude-code
586			// emit colored stderr banners whose first line can be escape codes
587			// only. TrimSpace doesn't drop those, so without stripping we'd pick
588			// the chrome and hide the real message on subsequent lines.
589			for _, line := range strings.Split(pe.Stderr, "\n") {
590				trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(stripANSI(line))
591				if trimmed != "" {
592					return trimmed
593				}
594			}
595			if pe.Err != nil {
596				return pe.Err.Error()
597			}
598		}
599		return err.Error()
600	}

603		const (

605			statusWidth   = 10
606			durationWidth = 8
607			tokensWidth   = 8
608			minWidth      = agentWidth + statusWidth + durationWidth + tokensWidth + 8 // four two-space separators
609		)
610		termWidth := m.dashboardWidth()
611	
612		previewWidth := termWidth - minWidth
613		if previewWidth < 0 {
614			previewWidth = 0
615		}
616	
617		line := fmt.Sprintf("%s  %s  %s  %s  %s",
618			padDisplayWidth(agent, agentWidth),
619			padDisplayWidth(status, statusWidth),
620			padDisplayWidth(duration, durationWidth),
621			padDisplayWidth(tokens, tokensWidth),
622			truncateDisplayWidth(preview, previewWidth))
623		return truncateDisplayWidth(line, termWidth)
624	}

628		succ, fail, canc := 0, 0, 0
629		for _, r := range m.summary.AgentRuns {
630			switch r.Status {
631			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded:
632				succ++
633			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed:
634				fail++
635			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled:
636				canc++
637			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown:
638				// not counted
639			}
640		}
641		return fmt.Sprintf("%d agent(s) done — %d succeeded, %d failed, %d cancelled",
642			len(m.summary.AgentRuns), succ, fail, canc)
643	}

647		if d < time.Second {

649		}
650		if d < time.Minute {

653		return fmt.Sprintf("%dm%ds", int(d.Minutes()), int(d.Seconds())%60)

content.text: Tasks already track the right structure — keeping them. Continuing the deeper exploration the user asked for.

I've now reviewed everything. Confirming the remaining gaps:

**Tokens-only-at-end is a parser limitation**, not a UI bug. The TUI dashboard already has a live TOKENS column (`tui_model.go:291`) — but the agents' parsers only emit a single `Tokens{}` event when the run finishes (`claudecode/reviewer.go:126` on `case "result"`, `codex/reviewer.go:157` on `turn.completed`). Claude's stream actually has per-message `usage` deltas we ignore.

**No "alt+" references** in the review code. All keybind labels say `Ctrl+…`/`enter`/`Esc` — they work on Mac but don't *look* Mac-native. The user's "alt accidentally" line may have been pointing at huh's defaults rather than our copy.

**Install hint highlighting** is literal backticks in the strings (`registry.go:48-71`) — huh's Note doesn't render them as code; they just sit there as literal characters, which is what looked "weird" in the screenshot.

You're right that workflow-first is the better frame. Here's how I'd describe the **entire workflow** as it exists today, then I want to lay out three different mental-model directions to discuss before touching commands or mockups:

## What `entire review` actually does today, end-to-end

1. **First-run setup**: a serial loop of huh forms — one form per installed agent, each with 4 fields (built-ins, plugin skills, install-more hint, freeform instructions). After the loop, one more form asks "choose fix agent" (a third concept that wasn't framed upfront).
2. **Run**: dispatches to single- or multi-agent path based on the configured set; spawns agent process(es) with `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` env vars; tags the session as a review via the lifecycle hook.
3. **Display**: TUI dashboard during the run, dump-style narrative at the end, optional cross-agent synthesis (y/N).
4. **Persistence**: review session is condensed into the next checkpoint on commit; no commit, no permanence.
5. **Findings**: `--findings` browses a local manifest file written after each run (`.entire/review/*.json`).
6. **Fix**: `--fix` lets the user pick sources and findings from that manifest and **launches another agent process** with a fix prompt.
7. **Attach**: post-hoc tag an existing session as a review (for agents that don't subprocess-launch).

So conceptually there are **five jobs in one verb**: configure, review, view findings, fix findings, attach. Plus the "fix agent" concept lurking inside configure as a sub-concept.

## Three workflow mental models worth discussing

Let me describe these in text before mocking anything. Each has a different answer to the core question: *"what is the user's primary loop?"*

---

**Model A — Review-and-fix as one continuous flow** *(most like the current code, polished)*

Primary loop: `entire review` does the whole thing. After running review, it offers "Found 7 findings. Fix them now?" right there in the same session. Skills configure on first run via a simpler form; fix-agent picker is dropped (default to the alphabetically-first launchable agent in the configured set; let `--fix-agent` override). Setup is one screen instead of N.

The "next: ..." style still applies but as in-flow nudges, not separate commands.

---

**Model B — Roles are first-class** *(addresses the "clunky 'claude reviews, codex fixes'" complaint head-on)*

Setup asks one question first: **what role does each agent play?** "Reviewer", "Fixer", or "Both". Then it only asks about review skills for agents that have the reviewer role. The fix-agent concept disappears as a separate step because it's just "the agent whose role is Fixer (or Both)". Run uses reviewers; `--fix` uses the fixer. Mixed assignments fall out naturally.

---

**Model C — clawpatch-style noun-verb subcommands** *(biggest restructuring)*

`entire review setup` / `entire review run` (or just `entire review`) / `entire review findings` / `entire review fix` / `entire review attach`. Each prints `next: entire review …` at the end. Each step has its own artifact (config file, findings manifest, patch attempt). Setup is its own command, so the first-run picker no longer interrupts "I just want to run a review."

This and Model B compose well — you could do roles-first setup AND noun-verb subcommands.

---

So before I propose specific designs and start mocking, the real fork is:

**Setup**: subcommand mechanically (`entire review setup`) but borrow Option 1's footer callouts (`# Only Reviewers get asked for skills next. # Fixer is used by entire review fix.`) for context.

**Saved state**: also include `Edit later: entire review setup` after saving (no `--setup` flag — the verb is its own command).

**Run output**: keep the live tokens column populated mid-run (this is the parser fix on the agent side — read per-message `usage` deltas instead of only the final result envelope).

**Commit attaches**: keep "Review session attached to checkpoint …" line as-is.

## On the "one fixer" question

Yes — **only one fixer**, and I think the cleanest role model is:

| Role | How many | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Reviewer | N (multiple) | Runs in parallel when `entire review` is invoked |
| Fixer | 1 | The agent `entire review fix` uses |
| Both | 1 | Reviews AND is the fixer (counts toward the one-fixer cap) |
| Skip | N | Not used by review |

Reason: review reads, fix writes. Reads can fan out (multi-agent review is already supported); writes can't (two fixers racing on the same file diverges). The setup form would enforce: at most one of {Fixer, Both} across the agents. If the user tries to set two Fixers, the second pick auto-demotes the first one to Reviewer with a small inline note.

Side benefit: removes the "Choose fix agent" prompt entirely — the fixer is just whoever has that role. That solves the "what is fix agent?" confusion from your original list.

## Scene 6 — the discussion point

You said you're torn between Option 1's inline `[Y/n]` and Option 2's `Run: entire review fix` pointer. Here's a hybrid that does both, plus uses the `[A]` shortcut convention you've baked in:

```
Review complete — 7 findings.
Report: .entire/review/2026-05-19-1432.md

  1. Missing input validation       auth.go:23
  2. SQL injection risk             queries.go:88
  3. Race condition in cache lookup cache.go:142
  …4 more

Fix now with Codex? [Y]es · [n]o · [p]ick which · [A]lways

# After "n":
  Run later: entire review fix
                            (or: entire review fix --all)
```

- `Y / enter` → fix runs immediately (Option 1's feel)
- `n` → print the `Run later:` pointer (Option 2's pattern)
- `p` → multi-select picker for which findings (current `--fix` behaviour without `--all`)
- `A` → "Always fix" — sets `fix_after_review: always` in settings; next time skips the prompt and just runs fix. Matches your `[A] = Always apply` convention.

**For CI / non-TTY**: skip the prompt; print `Run later:` directly. So `entire review` in a CI run never blocks.

I think this gives you the best of both. The subcommand still exists for power users, the inline prompt covers the common case, and `[A]` lets people pre-commit to "yes, always fix" without re-prompting.

---

Two things I'd like a yes/no on before I draft the full design doc:

1. **Roles model**: Reviewer (N) / Fixer (1) / Both (1) / Skip — good?
2. **Scene 6**: the `[Y]es · [n]o · [p]ick · [A]lways` inline prompt with `Run later:` fallback — good, or do you want pure subcommands (drop the inline prompt entirely)?

And want me to push a consolidated **v4 mockup** that reflects all this feedback so you can sanity-check it visually?

okay better. For scene 3, i think currently we have like a settings level prompt then we also have a per run prompt, which i don't see built in. And then i assume in scene 4, there woudl be like comma separated list of agents if applicable. this one,  Browse later: entire review findings

there should be no extra indent and browse later sounds strange. also should we do choose fix or select fix? Everything else looks good

content.text:
Good catches. Let me address each and update v4.

**On `[c]hoose fix` vs `[s]elect fixes`** — my pick is `[s]elect fixes` (plural). "Select" is the established CLI verb for multi-pick lists (also matches `huh.NewSelect`/`MultiSelect`), and pluralizing "fixes" makes it obvious you're toggling individual findings, not flipping one global switch. If you'd rather keep `[c]hoose`, easy flip.

**On the per-run prompt** — you're right, I dropped it. The per-run prompt should be a flag on `entire review` (and `entire review fix`), not part of setup. So `entire review --prompt "focus on auth"` threads through to the agents for that one run only. Adding a dedicated scene that shows it.

**On scene 4 reviewer list** — yes, comma-separated when multiple. The setup form lets multiple agents have the Reviewer role, so the saved-state banner needs to print a list.

**On scene 7 `Browse later`** — rewriting to flush-left, dropping the awkward verb. New layout:

```
Skipped. Findings preserved.

Run:  entire review fix          apply when ready
      entire review fix --all    apply all without picker
      entire review findings     browse the findings
```

One "Run:" verb, three alternatives, no extra indent, every command flush under the first.

Making these edits now.

content.text:
Ah — that's the missing piece. Confirmed in `fix.go:597-605`: `entire review fix` calls `launcher.LaunchCmd(...)` and `cmd.Run()` — which **opens the agent's interactive CLI** (e.g., `codex` or `claude` in its native UI) with the fix prompt threaded in as the first message. It's not a stream-json subprocess like `entire review` is.

So my scene 8 was completely fictional — I was showing a streamed `codex ✓ done · tokens` row, but in reality the agent's full native CLI takes over the terminal until the user exits it. That's why the duplicate prompt felt weird: there isn't actually a clean "outcome row" — it's a handoff.

This also clarifies the redesign question. Two options:

**Option A — keep current behavior (interactive handoff)**: `entire review fix` opens the agent CLI like today. Mockup should show a clear "Codex took over, did stuff, came back" handoff panel, not a streamed-output row.

**Option B — unify with review (stream-json)**: `entire review fix` ALSO runs the agent headless via stream-json, with the same TUI dashboard as review. Same UX for review and fix. But: fix often needs interaction (the agent might want to ask "this looks ambiguous — clarify?"), and stream-json makes back-and-forth hard.

I'd recommend **A** — it preserves the established interactive feel for fixes, where you might want to redirect the agent mid-flight. We just need the mockup to honestly show the handoff.

Proposed combined scene 7 (replacing current 7+8) with the handoff made explicit:

```
Review complete — 7 findings. Apply now with Codex?
Report: .entire/review/2026-05-19-1432.md

  1. Missing input validation       auth.go:23
  2. SQL injection risk             queries.go:88
  3. Race condition in cache lookup cache.go:142
  …4 more in report

  [Y]es · [s]elect fixes · [n]o · [A]lways  y

╭─ codex ──────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Applying 7 fix proposals from review…        │
│ ✓ auth.go      ✓ queries.go    ✓ cache.go    │
│ ✓ middleware.go    ✓ db.go                   │
│ ⚠ session.go   (ambiguous — left for human)  │
│ ⚠ logging.go   (needs domain context)        │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Codex finished. 5 of 7 fixes applied · 2 skipped (manual review needed).

Run: git commit -am "review: apply 5 fixes"
```

One scene, no duplicate prompt, the `╭─ codex ─╮` panel makes the handoff visually obvious, then entire's `Run:` pointer at the bottom. Total = 8 scenes (was 9).

Want me to apply this? And do you agree with A over B for the fix execution model?

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.
   - Provide: chunk content, path to spec document
2. If ❌ Issues Found:
   - Fix the issues in the chunk
   - Re-dispatch reviewer for that chunk
   - Repeat until ✅ Approved
3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Ready to execute?"**

**Execution path depends on harness capabilities:**

**If harness has subagents (Claude Code, etc.):**
- **REQUIRED:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Do NOT offer a choice - subagent-driven is the standard approach
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If harness does NOT have subagents:**
- Execute plan in current session using superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

content.text:
Plan references and structure are accurate. Now drafting the review.

## Plan Review - Chunk 1

**Status:** Issues Found

**Issues:**

- **Task 1.4, Step 3 — Migration persistence is under-specified.** The plan introduces `persistMigratedSettings(ctx, settings)` with the hand-wave "See `Save` for an example", but there is no `Save` function visible in `settings.go` (only `SaveClonePreferences`). The user's settings may live in `settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, or `entire/preferences.json` (clone-local). The plan does not specify which file gets the migrated roles written back, nor how to handle the legacy `review_fix_agent` field after migration (delete it? leave it for compat?). This is a real design question, not a 2–5 minute step.

- **Task 1.4 — Migration-on-load behavior is risky and not justified.** Auto-persisting a settings file on every `settings.Load` call (which happens many times per CLI invocation) could race with concurrent invocations or write files the user didn't expect. The plan should either gate persistence (idempotent guard via a version field) or make migration in-memory only with a one-time persist on the first command that mutates settings (e.g., `entire review setup`).

- **Task 1.3 + 1.4 — Duplication is acknowledged but not resolved.** Step 4 of Task 1.4 says "keep both ... the duplication is small and the test surface stays". This contradicts CLAUDE.md's "Code Duplication Prevention" section (75-token lint threshold). The migration body is ~25 lines and would likely trip `dupl`. Better resolution: keep the canonical logic in `settings/migration.go`, and have `review.MigrateLegacyRoles` be a one-line wrapper (`return settings.MigrateLegacyRoles(s)` after exporting it).

- **Task 1.2, Step 4 — Vague `ClonePreferences` instruction.** "Check `ClonePreferences` at line 125; mirror the field if needed — keep symmetric with `ReviewFixAgent`." This is a "similar to X" non-actionable step. The plan should commit: either add `FixAfterReview` to `ClonePreferences` or don't. (Symmetry with `ReviewFixAgent` argues yes.)

- **Task 1.4, Step 1 — Test imports missing.** The test uses `context`, `os`, `filepath`, `testutil` but the plan doesn't list the import block. Minor, but worth fixing since the chunk is otherwise meticulous.

**Recommendations:**

- Task 1.3's `FixerOf` test comment says "documents the tiebreaker" but the assertion accepts either result — that's not a tiebreaker test. Either assert `"codex"` (alphabetical) or drop the test.
- `NormalizeRoles`'s unused `winner` variable with `_ = winner` is a lint smell; just delete the line.
- Chunk size is ~595 lines — well under the 1000 cap.
- All tests correctly use `t.Parallel()`; `testutil.InitRepo` correctly used in Task 1.4.

## Plan complete and reviewed

**Saved to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-20-entire-review-redesign.md` (2243 lines, ~610 / 629 / 668 / 336 lines per chunk).

**Review status:** All 4 chunks **approved on iteration 2**. The plan-document-reviewer subagent caught 25+ issues on the first pass (missing imports, undefined helpers, copy-paste bugs, unclear migration strategy); all have been fixed. The plan is not committed to git (per your standing memory).

## What the plan delivers (4 logical commits)

1. **Settings schema + Role model + migration** — `Role` enum (Reviewer/Fixer/Both/Skip), `FixAfterReview` mode, `NormalizeRoles`/`MigrateLegacyRoles`/`ReviewersOf`/`FixerOf` helpers, idempotent in-memory migration on `Load` (no auto-write — persists lazily on next settings write).
2. **`entire review setup`** — two-step picker: role per agent → skills for Reviewers/Both only. Uses `huh.NewInput` (single-line) so plain ↩ submits. Banner with display labels.
3. **Run flow + inline prompts** — drop the auto-picker, drop the multi-agent picker, drop the "Choose fix agent" prompt, promote `--fix` to subcommand, add `--prompt` to both review and fix, inline per-run-prompt ask, end-of-review `[Y]/[s]/[n]/[A]` prompt with always-mode persistence. Post-review UX in new `post_review.go`. Copy switched from `Next:` to `Run:`.
4. **Live tokens** — Claude parses per-message `usage` deltas; Codex parses `item.completed` running usage. Fixture-backed tests plus Haiku smoke as the real verification.

## Next step

Per the writing-plans skill, the standard execution path is **superpowers:subagent-driven-development** (fresh subagent per task + two-stage review). That dispatches each task in the plan as its own short-lived subagent, runs the TDD steps, and stops at each commit boundary for you to review.

content.text:
## The problem it fixes

`entire review` is meant to be a regular CLI command, but in practice it gets invoked from inside *another* agent's CLI all the time — you're chatting with Claude Code or Codex, you ask it to "run entire review and explain what it finds", and the agent shells out to `entire review`.

That spawned `entire review` process has:
- **No real terminal** for stdin (the parent agent owns the TTY).
- **No way to drive an interactive form** like `entire review setup` (huh forms need keypresses).

Before this addition, the plan said: *"if no config exists, print `Run: entire review setup` and exit non-zero."* That works fine for a human at a terminal, but for an agent calling `entire review` blind, it's a dead end — the agent reads "Run: entire review setup", tries to run THAT, and hits the same wall (the setup form can't run either).

## How detection works

`interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` is the existing helper. It returns `false` when:
- The CLI was invoked from inside Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Copilot CLI, Pi (each sets a sentinel env var).
- `CI=true` (or similar).
- `/dev/tty` can't be opened (e.g., piped input).
- `testing.Testing()` is true (so tests are non-interactive by default).

So the same check that already gates "should I show a huh prompt?" also tells us "is a human here to run setup?"

## What auto-bootstrap does

When both conditions hold — **no config AND non-interactive** — instead of dying, the redesign synthesizes a sensible default:

- For every installed agent whose hooks are wired AND which can subprocess-launch (`agent.LauncherFor(...)` returns a launcher): assign role **Reviewer**.
- The alphabetically-first qualifier additionally gets role **Both** (so it doubles as the Fixer).
- Skills default to each agent's curated built-ins (`/review`, `/security-review`, etc. — the ones that ship with the agent, no plugin install required).

Then it prints one line to stdout:

```
Auto-configured review (no prior config detected). Reviewers: claude-code, codex. Fixer: claude-code. Run `entire review setup` from an interactive shell to customize.
```

The note serves two purposes: tells the agent reading the output what was assumed, and tells a human running it through CI/automation what to do if the defaults are wrong.

It also tries to persist the bootstrapped config (`settings.Save`) so the next run doesn't repeat the inference. If persistence fails (e.g., read-only filesystem), it logs a warning and continues with the in-memory config — best-effort.

## What it does NOT do

- It doesn't auto-bootstrap when there's a real terminal. Humans see `Run: entire review setup` as before — they should drive the picker themselves to get exactly what they want.
- It doesn't try to install plugins or change which agents are enrolled in `entire enable`. If no agents are installed at all, you still get an error ("run `entire enable` first").
- It doesn't ask the agent for input. The whole point is "no prompting" — the agent can't answer.

## The trade-off

Silent auto-defaulting is slightly opinionated — we're making choices on the user's behalf. The defense is:

1. The defaults are reasonable (everyone reviews, first one fixes).
2. The note explicitly says what was assumed, so nothing is hidden.
3. The alternative (hard error) makes the command unusable from inside agent CLIs, which is one of the main ways people will use it.

A user who hates the defaults can run `entire review setup` later — settings.Save persisted the bootstrap, so editing is the same flow as customizing any other config.

content.text:
Really good push — I think the auto-bootstrap is actually too aggressive and you're right to question it.

## Yes, technically it can — and that's the problem

If you ask me (Claude Code) to run `entire review` and the repo isn't configured:

- The spawned `entire review` process would, under the current plan, decide that **all installed launchable agents** are reviewers — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, whatever's there.
- It would then spawn each of those as a subprocess: `claude --output-format=stream-json`, `codex --json`, `gemini --json`.
- Each spawned agent makes its own API calls — billed to whoever owns the keys.
- The Claude Code instance you were chatting with kicks off **3 more agent runs** you never explicitly asked for.

That's a real surprise. "Run entire review" should not silently fan out to two paid services the user never configured.

## What the user actually asked

Probably one of:
1. "Have one agent review my changes" (any reasonable agent — probably the one I'm already talking to).
2. "Have the agents I configured review my changes" (only if they configured something).

Neither of those wants "spawn every launchable agent on my machine."

## Better approach — invoker-aware fallback

When `entire review` is non-interactive AND no config exists, **detect which agent is calling** and use only that one. The same env sentinels `CanPromptInteractively()` already checks (`CLAUDE_CODE`, `CODEX`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `COPILOT_CLI`, `PI_CODING_AGENT`) tell us who the caller is.

So if Claude Code calls `entire review` with no config:
- Reviewer = `claude-code` (the caller).
- Fixer = `claude-code` (role: Both — it can review and fix).
- Skills = its curated built-ins.
- Note: "No config — using claude-code (the calling agent). Run `entire review setup` from an interactive shell to fan out to multiple reviewers."

No other agent gets spawned. The user pays for what they already opted into.

If `entire review` is called from CI or piped output (no agent sentinel set) AND no config exists, fall back to one of:
- **Hard error** ("no config; run `entire review setup`"). Safest. CI scripts must opt in.
- Or alphabetical-first launchable. Like the old auto-bootstrap but only one agent, not all.

I'd lean hard error for the pure-CI case — a CI run that silently spawns Claude is also a surprise.

## Other safeguards worth adding

- **Recursion guard**: if `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION` is already set in the env, refuse to start a new review (the spawned agent already IS reviewing — calling `entire review` recursively is almost always a bug or a loop).
- **Cost ceiling per invocation**: an `ENTIRE_REVIEW_MAX_AGENTS=1` env var that overrides the configured roles when set. Useful guardrail in agent contexts.

## Want me to amend the plan?

The change would be:
- `autoBootstrapReviewConfig` accepts the caller-agent name (or "") and uses ONLY that agent if known, OR errors with `Run: entire review setup` if unknown.
- Add a helper `detectInvokingAgent()` that reads the same env sentinels `interactive.CanPromptInteractively` checks.
- Add the recursion guard in `runReview`.

Want me to apply that, or rethink the non-interactive design differently?

Both are sharp. Let me address each:

## On checkpoint/session context

You're absolutely right that this is the differentiator. `entire review` doesn't just hand the diff to an agent — it threads:
- **Scope info** (commits/files changed since the base ref)
- **Checkpoint context** (`deps.ReviewCheckpointContext(...)` — the rolled-up prior session metadata at the current commit)
- **Session-level summaries** (which agents have already touched this code, prior review findings, etc.)

This happens regardless of whether config exists, interactively or not. Worth calling out explicitly in the mockup AND the plan — currently it's implicit.

## On inline role specification

Yes — this should be a first-class flag on `entire review` so the calling agent can translate user intent ("you review, codex fixes") into a concrete invocation. The cleanest shape is two flags:

- `--reviewers <comma-list>` — agents to use as reviewers for this run
- `--fixer <name>` — agent to use as fixer for this run

An agent in the chat overlay sees "you review and codex fixes" → composes:

```
entire review --reviewers claude-code --fixer codex
```

Rules:
- These **override** saved roles for this invocation only (not persisted).
- They work whether or not setup has run — so they also solve the no-config case more elegantly than auto-bootstrap.
- Validation: error if a named agent isn't installed; error if no reviewer specified; if `--fixer` matches a `--reviewers` entry, that agent gets `Both` semantics.

This collapses the decision tree to:

1. `--reviewers` / `--fixer` flags passed → use those (one-off).
2. Saved config exists → use it.
3. Interactive, no config → "Run: entire review setup".
4. Non-interactive, no config, invoking agent detected → use that agent as Reviewer+Fixer (Both).
5. Non-interactive, no config, no agent detected (CI) → hard error.

The `--reviewers`/`--fixer` path makes #4 mostly redundant — but #4 is still nice as a fallback if the agent forgets the flags.

content.text:
## Will it show up in agent sessions?

Yes. When Claude Code (or Codex, Gemini CLI) runs `entire review` as a subprocess, the subprocess's stdout is captured by the agent. Two things happen:

1. **The agent always sees the full text** in its context window — so even if the user never sees "Note: ..." verbatim, the agent reads it and can act on the cue.
2. **The user sees it too**, either verbatim (most agents pass subprocess output through to the chat) or summarized (the agent might paraphrase if it's verbose).

So whatever you write reaches both audiences — but the agent is your "smarter" reader, the human is the casual scanner.

## Should we include `--reviewers/--fixer`?

I think yes, but **subordinated** to the natural-language path. The flags help the agent know the exact CLI invocation when it translates the user's words. Humans skip past parentheticals.

My recommendation:

> Note: claude as reviewer + fixer (no config detected).
> To customize: run `entire review setup`, or ask your agent to use specific agents (it'll re-invoke with `--reviewers/--fixer`).

This:
- Humans read "ask your agent to use specific agents" as the natural path.
- The agent reading the same line sees `--reviewers/--fixer` and knows the literal invocation.
- Doesn't ask the human to memorize flag names.

If you want it as one line:

> Note: claude as reviewer + fixer (no config). Customize with `entire review setup`, or tell your agent who should review/fix (it'll re-invoke with `--reviewers/--fixer`).

content.text:
Yes — exactly. This is the core motivation for `--reviewers` being a list. The invocation is:

```
entire review --reviewers codex,claude-code --fixer codex
```

Codex (the calling agent) translates the user's English into that single command. Internally `entire review`:

1. Resolves reviewers = `[codex, claude-code]`, fixer = `codex`.
2. Since `codex` appears in BOTH lists, it implicitly gets Role `Both`. (claude-code = Reviewer.)
3. Spawns the two reviewers in parallel via the existing `RunMulti` — each gets its own subprocess, stream-json output, live token row in the TUI.
4. Aggregates findings into one manifest.
5. Inline fix prompt: *"Apply N fixes now with Codex?"* → on `[Y]` (or auto-resolved by the calling Codex), Codex opens with the consolidated fix prompt.

## Flag shape

`--reviewers` accepts a comma-separated list, e.g. `--reviewers codex,claude-code,gemini-cli`. (Cobra's `StringSliceVar` also accepts repeatable form `--reviewers codex --reviewers claude-code` for free — both work.) No artificial N-cap.

## A few safety notes for this case specifically

- **Recursion guard:** when outer Codex runs `entire review`, the spawned `entire review` sets `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION` in the env of each child reviewer. If an inner agent tried to call `entire review` again from its review prompt, the guard refuses (otherwise: infinite fan-out). Plan already includes this guard.
- **No double-spawn of the calling agent:** outer Codex (the chat) and inner Codex (the reviewer) are separate processes. Outer Codex's session keeps running normally; inner Codex is launched fresh, runs the review skill against the diff, and exits. Two billed Codex calls but no session collision.
- **Fixer = one of the reviewers is fine:** Codex reviews AND fixes is Role `Both`. The fix step opens AFTER both reviewers finish, so Codex's reviewing session is already done when its fixing session starts — no contention.

So: yes, this flow works today's-architecture, and `--reviewers` as a list is the right surface.

content.text:
Yes — any combination is supported, and the output adapts to match what the user asked for. The two flags compose freely:

- `--reviewers <list>` = who reviews (1+ agents)
- `--fixer <name>` = who fixes (0 or 1 agent; same agent allowed in both)

| User says in Codex | Codex composes | Role inference | What user sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| "claude reviews and fixes" | `--reviewers claude-code --fixer claude-code` | Claude = Both | TUI row: claude-code · Fix prompt: *"Apply N fixes with Claude?"* |
| "you review, codex fixes" *(said to Claude)* | `--reviewers claude-code --fixer codex` | Claude = Reviewer, Codex = Fixer | TUI: claude-code only · Fix prompt: *"Apply N fixes with Codex?"* |
| "you and Claude review, you fix" *(to Codex)* | `--reviewers codex,claude-code --fixer codex` | Codex = Both, Claude = Reviewer | TUI: 2 rows · Fix prompt: *"Apply N fixes with Codex?"* |
| "Gemini reviews only" | `--reviewers gemini-cli` *(no `--fixer`)* | Gemini = Reviewer | TUI: gemini-cli · No fix prompt — prints *"Findings ready. Re-run with `--fixer <agent>` to apply, or browse: entire review findings"* |

## Where the output adapts

Three places key off the resolved roles, so users see exactly what they asked for:

1. **Scope banner + TUI dashboard** — only Reviewers appear as rows. If Codex isn't reviewing, no Codex row during the run.
2. **Inline fix prompt** — header reads `"Apply N fixes now with <Fixer's display label>?"`. So "Apply with Claude?" vs "Apply with Codex?" reflects who the user named.
3. **Final commit pointer** — same commit pointer either way; the review session metadata records which agents ran in which role, so the checkpoint can be inspected later.

## Edge case: no `--fixer`

If the user explicitly omits the fixer ("just review, don't fix yet"), the inline prompt is suppressed and the output ends with:

```
Findings ready. To apply: re-run with --fixer <agent>, or browse: entire review findings.
```

No nag, no setup hint — they got exactly what they asked for.

So yes: the flag surface is fully composable, and the rendered UI follows the roles, not a fixed template.

helper functions in picker.go.

## Plan Review - Chunk 3 (Iteration 3)

**Status:** Approved

**Resolved issues from iteration 2:**

All five CRITICAL items verified resolved:

- `resolveRolesFromFlags` (Task 3.1, Step 4) has a concrete body: builds `installedSet`, validates each `--reviewers` entry, assigns `RoleReviewer`, then assigns the `--fixer` agent `RoleBoth` when it also appears in reviewers (`if _, alsoReviews := reviewerSet[fixer]; alsoReviews`) or `RoleFixer` otherwise. At-most-one fixer enforced by `StringVar` (not slice).
- `detectInvokingAgent` (Task 3.3, Step 3) reads exactly the five documented sentinels: `CLAUDE_CODE`, `CODEX`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `COPILOT_CLI`, `PI_CODING_AGENT`, mapping each to its registry name.
- Recursion-guard test (Task 3.2, Step 1) asserts `strings.Contains(stderr.String(), "already in a review session")`, which matches the implementation's `"Already in a review session — refusing to start a nested review."` message (case-insensitive substring would also match; the literal lower-case substring is present verbatim).
- `userExplicitlyOmittedFixer bool` is the final parameter of `RunPostReviewFixPrompt` (Task 3.8, Step 2) and is set at the call site in `cmd.go` as `userExplicitlyOmittedFixer := len(reviewersFlag) > 0 && fixerFlag == ""`.
- Old auto-bootstrap tests are gone; the new tests are `TestRunReview_UnconfiguredInteractive_PrintsSetupPointer`, `TestRunReview_UnconfiguredNonInteractive_InvokerDetected_UsesInvokerOnly`, `TestRunReview_UnconfiguredNonInteractive_NoInvoker_HardError`, and `TestDetectInvokingAgent_ReadsEnvSentinels` — covering interactive, invoker-detected, no-invoker, and the env-sentinel mapping respectively. The invoker-detected test explicitly asserts that codex is NOT included in the run, locking in the "no surprise spawns" goal.

**Verification matrix:**

| Category | Result |
|---|---|
| Completeness | Pass — no TODO/TBD/placeholder strings in chunk 3. |
| Spec alignment | Pass — flags + invoker-only fallback match the stated design. |
| Task decomposition | Pass — Task 3.1 (flags), 3.2 (recursion), 3.3 (fallback) are properly separated; each has its own TDD cycle. |
| File structure | Pass — `setup.go` for helpers, `cmd.go` for flag declarations, `post_review.go` for end-of-run UX. |
| Task syntax | Pass — checkboxes `- [ ]` used throughout, no spurious checked boxes. |
| Numbering | Pass — Task 3.1–3.11 consecutive at lines 1307/1438/1482/1680/1745/1847/1906/2013/2223/2267/2288. |
| Chunk size | 1038 lines, ~4% over the 1000-line cap. Splitting would violate the 1–4-commits-per-PR rule. Acknowledged. |

**New issues:** None.

**Recommendations (advisory):**

1. Task 3.3, Step 3: the `_ = (*strings.Reader)(nil)` import-pin in `inline_prompt.go` (Task 3.7) is a code smell — `strings` is used in normal code paths via `strings.TrimSpace` elsewhere; if not, drop the import rather than pinning it. Minor.
2. Task 3.3, Step 4: the call to `settings.Save(ctx, s)` after invoker-only fallback persists what was intended as a one-off bootstrap. If a user runs once inside Claude Code and later opens the repo from Codex, the saved Claude-Both config will silently win over invoker detection. Consider not persisting (matches the `--reviewers/--fixer` "not persisted" rule) or printing a clearer note that config was saved. Optional.
3. Task 3.3 test `TestDetectInvokingAgent_ReadsEnvSentinels`: the loop sets each env var then clears it via `t.Setenv(c.envKey, "")`, but `t.Setenv("", "")` doesn't unset — it sets to empty, which `detectInvokingAgent`'s `!= ""` check correctly treats as absent. Functionally fine; just noting that prior sentinels in the loop persist as empty strings.

message.content: this is a huge refactor, so does this require separate pr

content.text:
Honest answer: yes, splitting into 2 PRs is the right call. The chunks split cleanly along a "foundation vs. cutover" line:

## Recommended split

**PR 1 — Foundation (pure-additive, no user-visible change)**
Chunks 1 + 2 = ~1240 lines of plan = 2 commits:
- Settings schema (Role enum, FixAfterReview, migration)
- New `entire review setup` subcommand

Nothing existing changes. `entire review` keeps working exactly as today (saved configs without roles get migrated in-memory; the new setup verb just exists alongside). A user could run this PR's code and notice nothing different unless they go looking. Safe to land.

**PR 2 — Cutover (user-visible behavior change)**
Chunks 3 + 4 = ~1320 lines of plan = 2 commits:
- Drop the old auto-picker, add `--reviewers/--fixer` flags, invoker-aware fallback, recursion guard, inline post-review fix prompt
- Live token parser updates

This is the behavioral change. Comes after PR 1 lands and depends on the new settings fields + setup subcommand existing.

## Why 2 PRs beats 1 or 3+

- **vs 1 PR (everything together):** 2620 lines of plan, ~10 modified files, ~8 new files. That's a lot to hold in a reviewer's head. Splitting halves the cognitive load and lets reviewers approve the safe foundation quickly.
- **vs 3+ PRs (one per chunk):** chunk 1 alone delivers no value to users — it's just plumbing. Same for chunk 4 (live tokens are a nice tweak, not a feature). Pairing them with their natural partner (chunk 1 with chunk 2; chunk 4 with chunk 3) makes each PR a complete unit.

## A few practical notes

- **Order matters**: PR 2 can't merge until PR 1 lands (chunk 3 uses helpers from chunk 1 and chunk 2). Keep that in mind when scheduling.
- **Each PR still has 2 commits** — within your "1-4 commits per PR" preference.
- **If you want to be even more conservative**, PR 2 could ship behind a feature flag (env var `ENTIRE_REVIEW_V2=1`) and you can A/B test before flipping the default. Worth it only if you have anxious users.

Want me to update the plan to call out the PR boundaries explicitly (e.g., add an "## How to land this" section at the top), or leave the plan as-is and just remember the split when executing?

Yes — all the non-interactive support lives in **chunk 3, which is PR 2**:

- **Task 3.1** — `--reviewers`/`--fixer` flags (the primary way an agent in a CLI translates user intent into a non-interactive invocation)
- **Task 3.2** — recursion guard (`ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION` env check, prevents fan-out loops when a reviewer agent's prompt accidentally tries to re-invoke review)
- **Task 3.3** — invoker-aware fallback (`detectInvokingAgent`, `invokerOnlyReviewConfig`)
- **Tasks 3.5–3.8** — the inline per-run-prompt ask + inline fix prompt, both of which gate on `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` and silently skip when non-interactive

PR 1 (foundation) is pure-additive — it adds settings fields, the migration, and the new `setup` subcommand, but it **doesn't change the run flow at all**. So between PR 1 landing and PR 2 landing:

- Non-interactive callers behave exactly as today (some kind of failure when no config exists, the old auto-picker can't render).
- Interactive callers also behave as today (legacy picker still fires on `entire review` with no config).
- The new `entire review setup` subcommand works as expected for both.

No intermediate state where things get *worse*. PR 2 then fixes the non-interactive story properly.

If you ever needed to ship PR 1 and pause indefinitely before PR 2 (unlikely), one defensive option would be to add a tiny shim in PR 1 that prints `Run: entire review setup` *only when non-interactive with no config* — basically a 5-line preview of PR 2's logic, no flags or roles required. But honestly not worth the complexity if PRs land close together.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Two-stage review after each task: spec compliance first, then code quality
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [shape=box];
        "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer subagent asks questions?";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?";
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?";
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [label="yes"];
    "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Prompt Templates

- `./implementer-prompt.md` - Dispatch implementer subagent
- `./spec-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch spec compliance reviewer subagent
- `./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Extract all 5 tasks with full text and context]
[Create TodoWrite with all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Get Task 1 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: "Got it. Implementing now..."
[Later] Implementer:
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant - all requirements met, nothing extra

[Get git SHAs, dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Approved.

[Mark Task 1 complete]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Get Task 2 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: [No questions, proceeds]
Implementer:
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Self-review: All good
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ❌ Issues:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  - Extra: Added --json flag (not requested)

[Implementer fixes issues]
Implementer: Removed --json flag, added progress reporting

[Spec reviewer reviews again]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant now

[Dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Solid. Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Implementer fixes]
Implementer: Extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant

[Code reviewer reviews again]
Code reviewer: ✅ Approved

[Mark Task 2 complete]

...

[After all tasks]
[Dispatch final code-reviewer]
Final reviewer: All requirements met, ready to merge

Done!
```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

## Integration

**Required workflow skills:**
- **superpowers:using-git-worktrees** - REQUIRED: Set up isolated workspace before starting
- **superpowers:writing-plans** - Creates the plan this skill executes
- **superpowers:requesting-code-review** - Code review template for reviewer subagents
